q.intro.text: On this floor plan, one inch represents four feet. The bedroom's long wall is three and a half inches on the plan. How long is the real wall? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one, and watch the plan first, then the maths on the board.

e.step0.text: The scale is a promise: every inch on the plan stands for four feet of the real room. The ruler shows it. Under each inch, four more feet.

e.step1.text: Measure the wall on the plan: from the zero mark to three and a half inches.

e.step2.text: Three and a half inches is three and a half groups of four feet. Three and a half times four is fourteen feet. Under the ruler, three and a half inches sits halfway between twelve and sixteen feet.

e.step3.text: Every length uses the same scale. The short wall is two and a half inches, so it is two and a half times four: ten feet. And the corners stay square. A scale drawing changes lengths, never angles.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is the real wall fourteen feet, and not six and a half feet?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. The scale multiplies. Each inch is four feet, so three and a half inches are three and a half times four: fourteen feet.

e.why.add.text: From one to four looks like add three. But the scale says each inch is four feet. Adding three only works for exactly one inch.

e.why.div.text: Dividing makes the real wall shorter than the drawing. The real room is bigger, so multiply by four.

t.intro.text: Now a school garden, drawn at one centimeter represents three meters. I'll do the first two steps. Then it's your turn.

t.given.text: Every centimeter on the plan is three meters of garden. The long side measures six centimeters on the plan.

t.long.text: How long is the real long side?

t.long.ok.text: Right. Six times three is eighteen meters.

t.long.add.text: One centimeter to three meters is not add two. It is times three. Each of the six centimeters stands for three meters.

t.long.div.text: The real garden is bigger than the plan. Multiply by three, don't divide.

t.long.same.text: Six is the length on the plan. Each centimeter of it stands for three meters.

t.long.miss.text: Each centimeter stands for three meters. Try again.

t.short.text: Same scale for every side. The short side is four point five centimeters on the plan. How long is it really?

t.short.ok.text: Right. Four point five times three is thirteen point five meters.

t.short.add.text: That adds instead of multiplying. Each of the four point five centimeters is three meters. Four point five times three.

t.short.div.text: The real side is longer than the drawing. Multiply by three.

t.short.miss.text: Four point five centimeters, three meters each. Try again.

t.shed.text: The school wants a shed that is six meters long. How long do you draw it on the plan?

t.shed.ok.text: Right. Six divided by three is two centimeters. From real to plan, you divide.

t.shed.times.text: That's six times three: a shed drawn bigger than the real one. From real to plan, divide by three.

t.shed.miss.text: How many groups of three meters fit in six meters? Try again.

t.done.text: Back to the bedroom. Each inch is four feet, so three and a half inches are three and a half times four: fourteen feet.

p.intro.text: Sam's plan uses one inch represents four feet. The room is three inches by two inches on the plan: six square inches. Sam says: the scale is four, so the real room is six times four, twenty-four square feet. Is Sam right?

p.build.no.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build.yes.text: Let's test it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true, and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: Every length is multiplied by four. The real room is twelve feet by eight feet.

p.c2.text: So the real area is twelve times eight: ninety-six square feet. Not twenty-four.

p.c3.text: One square inch of the plan stands for a square four feet by four feet: sixteen square feet. The area grows sixteen times, not four times.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. Lengths grow by the scale. Areas grow by the scale times the scale.

p.chip.area.text: That is exactly Sam's mistake. An area has two directions, and both of them grow.

p.chip.plan.text: The plan's numbers are inches on paper. The real room needs the scale.

p.chip.example.text: One room is an example, not a reason. Why does every square inch grow that much?

p.chip.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which one makes this line true?
